audit_notes: Physical check: air/water viscosity ratio 1.8e-5/1.22e-3 = 0.0148. Two-layer Couette gives effective slip b = h_a (mu_w/mu_a - 1) = 1.5e-3*66.8 = 0.10 m, i.e. >1000x the equivalent wall layer: under an intact air layer the local friction almost vanishes (99.9% in the laminar-equivalent model). Air-layer Reynolds number Re_a = U_d h_a / nu_a = 3.9*1.5e-3/1.5e-5 = 390 (laminar air film plausible). Measured local reductions in the air-layer regime are 80-90% (Elbing et al. 2008, HIPLATE), so the model overestimates the local effect by ~10-15%. Hull-level effect is obtained with metric.transform as area-weighted shear: (1 - A f) tau_0 + A f tau_air with bottom_area_fraction A=0.35 and covered_bottom_fraction f=0.5 -> expected gain ~17.5% of skin friction (upper bound; with 85% local DR it would be ~15%). Not included: compressor power (air flux ~0.05-0.1 m3/s per m of span at 15 kn with 10 m draft pressure ~1 bar -> several hundred kW to MW, typically 2-4% of propulsion power), loss of air at bilge keels/ roll, and the fact that the covered fraction 0.5 is an assumption, not a result. Capillary check: rib pitch 0.5 mm < capillary length 2.7 mm; Laplace pressure 2*gamma/pitch = 2*0.072/5e-4 = 290 Pa, far smaller than turbulent pressure fluctuations (~3 tau_w = 150 Pa rms, peaks >500 Pa) and hydrostatic head differences across the bottom, so the ribs pin the contact line only marginally; the stabilising claim is uncertain. Structural: silicone ribs 200 um high, 500 um pitch, no load issue. Simulation coefficient = effective slip length 0.10 m. Baseline: same hull without air layer (air_layer_thickness = 0) -> smooth FR wall.

performance_gain.label: Skin-friction reduction vs clean FR hull

hard_constraints: compressor power must be subtracted before a net fuel saving is claimed
